title: Why did South Korean stocks just crash?
gist: Noah Smith decomposes the KOSPI's round trip from ~5,000 to over 9,000 and back to ~5,500 into a genuine memory-chip earnings boom at SK Hynix and Samsung, and a retail leverage mania fueled by newly introduced leveraged single-stock ETFs. He argues the crash may also be the leading edge of a returning AI-bubble narrative, since AI revenue of roughly $150bn a year must grow ~17x to justify current data center capex and Chinese models like Kimi K3 are eroding the American moat.

insights.claim: The KOSPI index rose from around 5,000 to over 9,000 starting around March 2026, then reversed over roughly a month back to around 5,500.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sizes the round trip: an ~80% melt-up almost fully retraced, the signature of a leverage-driven move rather than a repricing of earnings.
insights.quote: the KOSPI index rose from around 5,000 to over 9,000
insights.locator: The Korean stock market has been crashing for weeks now

insights.claim: SK Hynix's operating profit went from under $10 billion in the first quarter of 2025 to over $35 billion in the first quarter of 2026, driven by AI data center demand for computer memory.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The fundamental leg of the Korean move is real — a 3.5x operating profit expansion in four quarters, which sets a very high bar for the next comparison.
insights.quote: SK Hynix’s operating profit went from under $10 billion in the first quarter of 2025 to over $35 billion in the first quarter of 2026
insights.locator: Only a few companies had the scale

insights.claim: Computer memory is normally a poor business — commoditized technology, brutal competition, enormous factory capital requirements, and risky long-term technology bets — but the AI boom converted it into an extraordinary one because only a few firms had the scale to meet the demand explosion.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The memory supercycle is a scarcity-of-scale rent, not a change in industry structure — it mean-reverts when capacity catches up or AI demand pauses.
insights.quote: Under normal circumstances, computer memory isn’t a great business to be in
insights.locator: For Korea, the fundamental story was about memory stocks

insights.claim: SK Hynix, a memory specialist, briefly attained a higher market capitalization than Samsung purely on the strength of the memory boom.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A pure-play memory name overtaking a diversified conglomerate is a classic late-cycle marker for a single-product boom.
insights.quote: Hynix, which specializes in memory, briefly had a higher market capitalization than Samsung, simply because the memory boom is so huge.
insights.locator: Hynix, which specializes in memory

insights.claim: South Korea's exports rose over 70% in a single year and the country's national GDP growth rate increased noticeably over two quarters because of one product category.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Korean macro data is now a high-frequency proxy for AI capex — a Korean export rollover would be an early global AI-demand signal.
insights.quote: Korea’s exports rose over 70% in just one year
insights.locator: Hynix, which specializes in memory

insights.claim: SK Hynix and Samsung rose +1,900% and +600% respectively in one year and at their peak accounted for as much as 50% of South Korea's entire stock market.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Index-level concentration of 50% in two AI-levered names means Korean equity beta was effectively a single AI trade.
insights.quote: These two stocks accounted for as much as 50% of South Korea's stock market last month.
insights.locator: Here’s a thread about just how epic the runup

insights.claim: Every big asset bubble combines a fundamental new-economy story with purely financial accelerants — noise traders with excess cash and opportunistic speculators riding sentiment — so the fundamentals explain direction while leverage explains magnitude and timing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A two-factor decomposition for any melt-up: check whether the marginal buyer is levered before concluding the fundamental story has broken.
insights.quote: But the big market movements are almost always accelerated by purely financial factors
insights.locator: There are probably two stories regarding why this happened

insights.claim: International investors mostly avoided the Korean memory boom; the most frenzied buyers were domestic Korean retail investors who likely did not understand the AI data center fundamentals and instead held extrapolative expectations.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Foreign underweight during the melt-up means the unwind is largely a domestic balance-sheet event, limiting direct cross-border contagion through positioning.
insights.quote: The most frenzied buyers were regular Korean people — the proverbial taxi drivers and teenagers.
insights.locator: This is where the financial story rears its head

insights.claim: The introduction of leveraged single-stock ETFs in Korea earlier in 2026 let ordinary savers with little spare cash effectively borrow to buy memory stocks, which is what turned retail enthusiasm into a market-moving flow.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Product innovation, not sentiment alone, was the transmission mechanism — watch new leveraged retail products as a bubble precondition in any market.
insights.quote: When you buy a share in a leveraged single-stock ETF in SK Hynix, it’s like borrowing money to buy SK Hynix stock.
insights.locator: Normal people don’t have a lot of cash sitting around

insights.claim: Leveraged ETFs mechanically amplify declines because falling prices force them to sell holdings, and simultaneous selling by many such funds pushes prices down further while separately triggering margin calls on levered individuals.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Explains why the Korean decline accelerated after late June and why forced-selling cascades overshoot fundamental value on the downside.
insights.quote: When a bunch of leveraged ETFs do this at the same time, it pushes prices down, forcing others to sell.
insights.locator: All that borrowed money accelerated the fall on the way down

insights.claim: Korea is now moving, belatedly, to restrict leveraged ETFs after the crash.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Regulatory restriction removes a structural bid from Korean single stocks, capping the speed of any recovery rally.
insights.quote: No wonder Korea is now moving — a little belatedly — to restrict leveraged ETFs.
insights.locator: It’s a very old story

insights.claim: The crash may have been triggered either by traders suddenly doubting the AI profit story or simply by Korea running out of hotheaded day traders willing to borrow more, meaning the influx of cash naturally halted with no news event required.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A bubble can top on exhaustion of marginal buyers alone — do not wait for a fundamental catalyst to de-risk a crowded levered trade.
insights.quote: The other possibility is that Korea simply ran out of hotheaded day traders willing to borrow more and more in order to bet on stocks
insights.locator: Then something happened last month

insights.claim: The 2025 AI bubble fear was resolved in 2026 when Claude Code demonstrated product-market fit for AI in writing computer code, with Anthropic emerging as market leader and cybersecurity and other zero-sum applications — where having the absolute best model matters — supplying the moat AI had previously lacked.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Identifies zero-sum, adversarial use cases as the structural moat for frontier labs — the segment to watch for pricing power.
insights.quote: Cybersecurity and other zero-sum applications — where having the absolute best model can matter a lot — started to seem like the “moat” that AI had previously lacked.
insights.locator: In 2026, Claude Code exploded onto the scene

insights.claim: Huge increases in coding productivity from AI are translating into only minor increases in the amount of software actually being shipped, according to Demirer et al. (2026).
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The key falsification test for the AI capex thesis — production output, not token consumption, is the metric that must inflect.
insights.quote: AI is amazing at writing software, but writing software is different from selling it.
insights.locator: But slowly, doubts have begun to creep back in

insights.claim: A significant fraction of the explosion in coding-agent usage may be 'tokenmaxxing' — companies burning AI capacity to learn the tools or to look like they are doing something — which would imply a retrenchment and a temporary slowdown in AI spending growth.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If enterprise token spend is partly experimental budget rather than production workload, inference demand forecasts and datacenter build schedules are overstated.
insights.quote: companies trying to use as much AI as they can, either to learn to use the tools, or perhaps just to look like they’re doing something
insights.locator: It’s possible that a significant fraction

insights.claim: The Economist estimates covering AI capex through identifiable AI income requires revenue on the order of $2.5 trillion a year — more than the entire combined revenue of tech today — against roughly $150 billion a year currently identifiable, with Anthropic at perhaps $75bn annualised, OpenAI at tens of billions, and Google, Microsoft, SpaceX and Meta making up the rest.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Quantifies the funding gap: AI revenue must compound roughly 17x to validate current capex, making revenue acceleration the single variable to track.
insights.quote: A back-of-the-envelope calculation finds that covering AI capex through identifiable AI income requires revenue on the order of $2.5trn per year, more than tech’s entire combined revenue today
insights.locator: Here’s a recent report from The Economist

insights.claim: Even the arrival of Claude Code is insufficient to justify current AI capital spending, because AI revenue must accelerate from its already fast growth rate by a further 17x.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the bull case as requiring a second discontinuity beyond coding — a single killer app does not close the capex gap.
insights.quote: it’ll have to grow by 17x from where it is now in order to justify the capital being spent
insights.locator: AI revenue is growing very fast

themes.theme: Chinese models erode the American moat

insights.claim: Chinese company Moonshot AI has released Kimi K3, a model that nearly equals the best available American models, and American companies are increasingly using cheap Chinese AI models for daily tasks.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Direct margin threat to US frontier labs in commodity workloads — monitor enterprise share shift toward Chinese open models.
insights.quote: A Chinese company called Moonshot AI has released a model called Kimi K3 that nearly equals the best available American models.
insights.locator: There’s also the possibility that the moat

insights.claim: If Anthropic and OpenAI lose the b2b market to cheap Chinese competition backed by Chinese subsidies and government support, they will be unable to pay for the data center boom, producing a bust comparable to the railroad failures of 1873.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Maps the tail scenario: infrastructure overbuild financed against revenues that get competed away — the classic mechanism of an industrial bust.
insights.quote: there could be a big, big bust — similar to when railroads went under in 1873
insights.locator: If Anthropic and OpenAI lose the overall b2b market

themes.theme: Contagion into the US AI complex

insights.claim: The selloff extends beyond Korea to Nvidia, Micron, Microsoft, Google and Amazon — the chip designers, memory makers and hyperscalers that build and run AI data centers.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Confirms the drawdown is an AI-complex repricing rather than a Korea-specific event, so hedges should target the AI capex chain broadly.
insights.quote: It isn’t just Korean AI-related stocks that have taken a hit recently.
insights.locator: Investors are probably already beginning to worry

insights.claim: The Magnificent 7 index is down 11% from a record reached in late May, erasing $2 trillion in market value, as investors grow cautious about Big Tech AI infrastructure spending with no visible return on investment.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete drawdown benchmark for the AI trade and evidence that the market's concern has shifted from capability to ROI.
insights.quote: The Mag 7 index is now down 11% from a record reached in late May, erasing $2 trillion in market value.
insights.locator: Here’s Bloomberg’s story about the decline

insights.claim: Situational Awareness, the $20bn hedge fund run by former OpenAI employee Leopold Aschenbrenner, rapidly sold a large portion of its public equity holdings after heavy losses, with Citadel stepping in to buy many of the stocks it was unloading.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Concentrated AI-thesis capital is being forced out and absorbed by mainstream multistrats — a positioning rotation that can extend the unwind.
insights.quote: Citadel — a big traditional mainstream finance firm — is now stepping in to buy many of the stocks owned by Situational Awareness.
insights.locator: Update: One possibility I should have mentioned

insights.claim: Korean retail investors are not the only ones using borrowed money to buy AI exposure — margin buying and leveraged ETFs are rising in America, and some large companies are themselves leveraging heavily.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The same leverage-cascade mechanism that broke the KOSPI is now present in the US AI complex, raising the risk of a similar non-linear unwind.
insights.quote: Derek flags the rise of margin buying and leveraged ETFs in America, but I also noticed that some pretty big companies are leveraging themselves to the teeth here
insights.locator: And as Derek Thompson noted a couple of weeks ago

insights.claim: Stock market movements exhibit excess volatility — prices move far more than warranted by changes in earnings or fundamental value — so all post-hoc explanations of a crash, including this one, deserve heavy discounting.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: An epistemic discipline for reading crash narratives: treat causal stories as hypotheses, and size positions on mechanism evidence like leverage data instead.
insights.quote: prices move up and down much more than is warranted by changes in earnings or other measures of fundamental value
insights.locator: Explaining stock market movements is always a little bit of a fool’s errand
